chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
title: Giving up clarinet for tenor; doubling clarinet and soprano
summary: He stopped playing clarinet as a feature when he stayed on tenor with Cliff Jackson, though section parts required clarinet and soprano.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Now, something we've jumped over, by this time you were playing tenor.
Now, when did you really make the break, when you laid the clarinet (unintelligible) down?
Well, I made the break, staying on the tenor, I went down there with Cliff Jackson.
That's when it happened. I didn't go back on alto any more. We used to play the clarinet together if you were a saxophone player, down there because at that time at a place you had to play clarinet.
You had to double on clarinet and B flat soprano.
Yes, certainly. You had to because we had these parts for it. You had parts for it, you had to play it. And you had to lug all that stuff with you.
Well, you used to play those clarinet trios.
Yeah, that was a pretty sound.
Pretty sound. When you got people who could play (unintelligible) when he played the clarinet.
That's right, because [—] were Earl was a very good clarinet players.
But what about the soprano? Did you find that hard or were you just sort of playing in the section sort of?
